mean: to brace oneself and stay focused
lit: to pull one's spirit tight, like tightening a loose belt or rope

near.diff: 気を取り直す is recovering your spirits after a setback; 気を引き締める is tightening your focus so you don't slip, often when things are going well.

mean: to have a hard time dealing with someone
lit: to burn one's hands: something is too hot to handle comfortably

near.diff: 手に負えない means it is beyond you altogether; 手を焼く means it is a struggle but you are still coping with it.

mean: to take measures, to act in time
lit: to make a move: te here is a step or means, as in a game, played against a problem

near.diff: 手を尽くす is trying every possible means; 手を打つ is taking a step against a problem, usually in time.

mean: to pull out of a deal or project
lit: to draw one's hand back from something one was holding

use.how: Xから手を引く: withdraw from a business, project or affair you were involved in. Literally, 子どもの手を引く also means to lead a child by the hand.

near.diff: 足を洗う is quitting a disreputable job or way of life for good; 手を引く is withdrawing from any project or affair.
手を抜く is doing a job carelessly; 手を引く is stopping your involvement altogether.

mean: to be more than one can handle

use.how: Xは(私の)手に負えない: a problem, task, child or situation is beyond one's ability or control. Also attributive: 手に負えない子.

near.diff: 手を焼く is struggling with something but still coping; 手に負えない says it is beyond you altogether.

ctx.en: "I can't fix the computer myself, so let's send it in for repair."

mean: to be on the edge of one's seat
lit: to clench one's fists until they are wet with sweat

use.how: Said by someone watching or following a tense situation unfold (a match, a film, a rescue). Often attributive: 手に汗を握る試合, also shortened to 手に汗握る.

near.diff: 息をのむ is a sudden gasp at a striking sight, beautiful or shocking; 手に汗を握る is sustained suspense over how something will turn out.

mean: to suddenly change one's attitude completely
lit: to flip one's hand over, palm up to palm down, in an instant

use.how: Usually 手のひらを返したように: someone turns on you, or suddenly fawns over you, when your fortunes change. Criticises opportunism.

near.diff: 気が変わる is simply changing one's mind; 手のひらを返す is an abrupt, self-serving reversal of attitude towards someone.

mean: to save someone's face, to let them keep their pride

mean: to watch someone's mood before acting

near.diff: 空気を読む is sensing the mood of a whole group or situation; 顔色をうかがう is watching one particular person, often anxiously.

cue: Before asking your father to borrow the car, you check whether he seems to be in a good mood after work.

ctx.s: 母[はは]の{顔色[かおいろ]をうかがって}から、お小遣[こづか]いの話[はなし]をした。
ctx.en: I checked what mood my mother was in before bringing up my pocket money.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]はいつも上司[じょうし]の{顔色[かおいろ]をうかがって}ばかりいる。
ctx.en: He's always watching the boss's face to see what he wants.

ctx.s: 「人[ひと]の{顔色[かおいろ]をうかがう}のはやめて、自分[じぶん]の意見[いけん]を言[い]いなさい。」
ctx.en: "Stop worrying about how people will react and say what you think."

ctx.s: 子[こ]どものころは、いつも父[ちち]の{顔色[かおいろ]をうかがいながら}暮[く]らしていた。
ctx.en: As a child, I lived always keeping an anxious eye on my father's moods.

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]は客[きゃく]の{顔色[かおいろ]をうかがいつつ}、新商品[しんしょうひん]を勧[すす]めた。
ctx.en: The shop assistant recommended the new product while gauging the customer's reaction.

ctx.s: 会議[かいぎ]では誰[だれ]もが社長[しゃちょう]の{顔色[かおいろ]をうかがい}、反対[はんたい]できなかった。
ctx.en: In the meeting everyone kept watching the president's expression, and no one could object.

bad.s: 医者[いしゃ]は患者[かんじゃ]の{顔色[かおいろ]をうかがって}、貧血[ひんけつ]だと言[い]った。
bad.en: (meant: the doctor looked at the patient's complexion and said he was anaemic)
bad.why: The idiom is reading someone's mood to decide how to act, not a medical look at skin colour. Say kaoiro o mite.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]はいつも上司[じょうし]に{顔色[かおいろ]をうかがう}。
bad.en: (meant: he is always watching his boss's mood)
bad.why: Whose face it is takes no, not ni: joushi no kaoiro o ukagau.
